nameStory: The cherry-faced meadowhawk gets its name from the deep cherry-red face that develops as these dragonflies mature. Like a ripening cherry turning from green to red, young cherry-faced meadowhawks start with paler faces that deepen to a rich, dark red color as they reach full adulthood. This rosy complexion makes them one of the more distinctive meadowhawks once you know what to look for.
description: The cherry-faced meadowhawk is a medium-sized dragonfly that's part of the skimmer family, those agile hunters you'll see patrolling low over fields and wetlands. Adults measure about an inch to an inch and a half long, with brown abdomens that turn dark red as they mature. Both males and females develop the characteristic cherry-red face that gives this species its name. Their wings are typically clear, though some females show amber coloring at the wing bases.

idTips.label: Cherry-red face
idTips.description: The mature face is deep cherry-red, almost burgundy in bright sunlight - much darker than the bright red of ruby meadowhawks

idTips.label: Black leg stripes
idTips.description: Legs are distinctly black, creating strong contrast against the reddish body when the dragonfly perches

idTips.label: Triangular side markings
idTips.description: Look for black triangular patches along the sides of the abdomen, like dark arrowheads pointing toward the tail

idTips.label: Dark red abdomen
idTips.description: The abdomen starts brown but deepens to dark red in mature individuals, with a somewhat matte finish rather than glossy

idTips.label: Wing coloration
idTips.description: Wings are usually clear in males, but some females have warm amber patches at the base near where wings attach to body

habitat: Cherry-faced meadowhawks prefer open areas near still or slow-moving water, including pond edges, marsh borders, and boggy areas throughout New England's lowlands and mid-elevations. You'll often spot them perching on low vegetation in sunny meadows, old fields, and wetland margins where they hunt for small flying insects. They're particularly fond of areas with cattails, sedges, and other emergent vegetation where they can easily launch hunting flights.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; larvae are developing underwater in ponds and marshes from eggs laid the previous fall.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season begins in mid to late summer, with freshly emerged adults showing brown faces and bodies that will redden with maturity.
seasonality.fall: Most active period extends well into fall when mature adults display their full cherry-red faces and engage in mating and egg-laying activities.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off; eggs overwinter in pond sediments and will hatch into aquatic larvae (nymphs) the following spring.

funFact: Cherry-faced meadowhawks are among the few dragonflies that actually get more colorful as autumn approaches - while leaves are turning red and orange, these dragonflies are also deepening from brown to rich red, creating a perfect camouflage match with fall foliage when they perch on dying vegetation.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with ruby meadowhawks, but cherry-faced have much darker, burgundy-red faces compared to ruby meadowhawks' bright cherry-red faces, plus those distinctive black triangular side markings. Memory trick: 'Cherry-faced has a darker cherry' - think of a deep, dark cherry versus a bright maraschino cherry.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'meadowhawk' refers to their hunting behavior of hawking (catching prey in flight) over meadows and open areas, similar to how hawks hunt. This is different from darners, which patrol territories, or clubtails, which prefer perching and ambushing prey.
compareHints: Cherry-faced meadowhawks are distinguished from other meadowhawks primarily by their very dark red, almost burgundy faces when mature, compared to the brighter reds of ruby meadowhawks or the white faces of white-faced meadowhawks. The black triangular side markings are more prominent than in most other meadowhawks. Unlike saffron-winged meadowhawks, cherry-faced typically have clear wings in males, and their leg coloration is uniformly black rather than striped.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, Autumn Meadowhawks are distinguished by their completely yellow legs - most other meadowhawks have black legs or black stripes on their legs.

Among New England meadowhawks, the band-winged is the only one with prominent dark wing bands - ruby meadowhawks have clear wings and bright red males, while autumn meadowhawks lack wing bands and have more orange-red coloring.
Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, the white-faced is the only one where males develop a pure white face - other meadowhawks have reddish, yellowish, or dark faces.

Among New England's meadowhawks, the Saffron-winged is most easily distinguished by its golden wing stripes in younger individuals and females, while the Ruby Meadowhawk typically shows clearer wings and the White-faced has a distinctly pale face.
